title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
content:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.
The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”
Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.
While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”
Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

report.summary: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic back a new IETF policy token in robots.txt letting publishers opt out of AI scraping across multiple companies at once.
report.background: AI companies have flooded the web with crawlers that collect content for model training and AI answers, prompting publishers to seek ways to limit access. The decades-old robots.txt file already tells crawlers whether they may index or archive a site, but AI training preferences have largely been handled company by company. Some publishers have turned to Cloudflare, which began blocking AI crawlers by default, or the Really Simple Licensing standard, which lets sites charge crawlers. Those approaches are fragmented and can be technically burdensome. The new proposal, led by Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley in the IETF, tries to create one shared signal that multiple AI providers can read and honor, reducing the need for publishers to negotiate or configure separate opt-outs for each company.
key_points: The proposed “policy token” would sit inside robots.txt and let a publisher express AI training preferences once. AI companies could read the same signal instead of requiring publishers to configure separate opt-outs for OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and others.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt the standard. Anthropic has already done so; Google and Microsoft plan support next year, while OpenAI says it will implement it in the coming months. Meta signaled support but did not commit to honoring the token.

Microsoft will offer granular choices to opt out of AI training or AI grounding—using content to verify answers—while keeping sites in Bing search results. Google has similar controls that separate AI search features and training from ordinary search visibility.

The move follows growing publisher frustration and alternative defenses such as Cloudflare’s default AI crawler blocking and RSL, which lets publishers charge crawlers. A common token could simplify compliance, but it remains a voluntary technical signal rather than a law or contract.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the shared token could become a default expectation for how crawlers respect publisher preferences, but adoption is voluntary and enforcement remains unclear. Developers building crawlers or AI search systems will need to parse the signal and decide how to handle training versus grounding. Publishers gain a simpler multi-company opt-out, yet opting out may reduce their presence in AI answers and future discovery channels. Regular users could see less publisher content in AI-generated responses, or more citations and links where grounding requires access. Google and Microsoft say ordinary search visibility should remain largely unaffected, but trust in the standard will depend on whether AI companies consistently honor it.
report.tools: Follow the IETF draft and robots.txt specifications; test how crawlers parse policy tokens with open-source robots.txt libraries. Watch Cloudflare’s AI crawler controls and bot management, and the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard for licensing or charging crawlers. Google’s AI controls in Search Console, Microsoft’s Bing Webmaster Tools, OpenAI’s GPTBot documentation, and Anthropic’s crawler documentation are useful for comparing implementations. For publishers, audit robots.txt and server logs to see which AI crawlers visit.
